title: The Effect Of Digestion And The Microbiome On Skin And Coat
summary: Long explainer on how digestion and the gut microbiome affect skin and coat condition, immunity and inflammation.
body:
The current flavour of the month when it comes to any discussion regarding **nutrition, skin and coat health, digestion and the function of the gut** is a full examination of the relevance of the microbiome. But what is the **microbiome** and what is all the fuss about?

**The gut microbiome is the collection of bacteria, fungi and viruses that inhabit the gastrointestinal tract (gut) of the pets,** and is not only responsible for many aspects of digestion but influences areas such as mood, disease resistance and well-being. The number of organisms that inhabit the gut is quite surprising; **there are more than a trillion of them and over a thousand species,** with the diversity of species in the microbiome being higher than that found in a rain forest. Some would claim “the microbiome should be classed as an organ”, or “our pets are 90% bacteria and 10% dog or cat”, but these statements are a little over the top. **The reality is the animal is approximately 50% animal and 50% microorganisms with each requiring the other for their survival.** In other words, the gut microbiome and the animal enjoy the ultimate symbiotic relationship.

## The Main Areas That Are Influenced By The Microbiome Are:

The immune system – up to 90% of the dog’s and cat’s immunity comes from the microbiome working in association with the mucous membrane lining of the gut. It is in this lining, known as **“gut-associated lymphoid tissues”**, where lymphocytes, T and B cells reside. These cells are the mainstay of the immune system and are **vitally important in providing immunity for the animal.**

## Mood

While we commonly think of the brain as being in the skull, what is not so widely known is there is a thin layer of brain cells embedded in the gut tissue and extending the full length of the gastrointestinal tract. Called the enteric system, these neurons are connected to the brain by the vagus nerve, which is a bit like a busy telephone line with messages zooming backwards and forwards all day long. But it’s via the vagus nerve that the **gut microbiota** appears to have a direct line to the brain, and can control mood by producing hormones such as the feel-good hormone dopamine and the neurotransmitter serotonin. Similarly, if your pet is consuming a disproportionate quantity of one foodstuff, such as sugars, the sugar-loving organisms will multiply and dominate, with the resultant craving (or fussy eating syndrome) for that type of food.

In one remarkable experiment with mice, researchers were able to show that mice infected with Toxoplasma gondii bacteria became strangely reckless and were strongly attracted to cat urine. When the bacterial balance was restored, the mice resumed their normal, cautious behaviour. It seems there is little doubt the Toxoplasma gondii bacteria were hell-bent on populating the cat’s microbiome by modifying the behaviour of the mice. Sounds far-fetched doesn’t it, but it is further confirmation of the “gut-brain axis” which is a popular subject of current research. Protection from disease-causing pathogens – a healthy microbiome protects the dog and cat by competitively excluding harmful bacteria and viruses. By completely colonising the gut, the good organisms out-compete the bad guys for food and starve them out. Full colonisation also severely limits the opportunities for the pathogens to gain a foothold in the gut from which to populate and expand.

## Forms a Protective Barrier

In the same way, as pathogens are excluded, the microbiome can form a protective layer that inhibits the absorption of harmful substances such as toxins, carcinogens, allergens and drugs, with these potentially dangerous substances being eliminated from the body in the faecal waste.

## Assists With Digestion while Producing Additional Nutrients

By far the most significant contribution the microbiome makes to the host animal is its assistance in releasing nutrients from the food, as well as producing other essential nutrients at the same time. One example of this is the production by the **microbiota of enzymes** to assist in the breakdown of the food, without which much of the nutrition contained in the food would not be able to be absorbed into the bloodstream. Once the nutrient breakdown is completed, **the microbiome assists in the transfer of the nutrients fro**m the gut to the bloodstream. Other members of the microbiome are responsible for the production of vitamins, particularly B vitamins, and while these are usually present in the food, the balance of the dog’s requirement is produced in the gut. **Another vital area is the fermentation of fibre by Bacteroidetes** to produce, amongst other substances, butyrate. Butyrate is an immensely important chemical in gut function because it not only helps to control the growth of cells in the wall of the gut and thus protects against bowel cancer but acts as an anti-inflammatory. While inflammation is the bodies key defence mechanism against infection, long term, low-level inflammation has an adverse effect on the body and is a precursor to many sensitivity and allergy issues in dogs and cats.

**This means the starting point in any discussion regarding skin and coat health must be the microbiome.** The presence of a long term, low-level gut inflammation causes the immune system to dramatically increase its level of activity, which in turn results in the immune system attacking simple compounds such as pollen and gluten. These attacks are an indication that the microbiome in its present state of diversity is ignorant of what substances are threatening, compared to the substances that pose no threat and can be left alone. It is also an indication that many of the species of organisms that evolved with the animal over millions of years have been lost, and with that loss is the **microbiome’s** knowledge as to which substances pose the real threat. This loss of beneficial organisms has been **exacerbated through the use of antibiotics, while stress, pollutants and highly processed foods all make a contribution.**

…the starting point in any discussion regarding skin and coat health must be the microbiome.

Unfortunately, we are seeing more and more dogs displaying skin sensitivity problems, with these problems appearing earlier in the dog’s life. Quite young pups are now regularly appearing with compromised skin and coat health, which suggests this loss of microbiome diversity is continuing unabated.

## So How Do We Reverse This Situation and Restore Good Health To Our Pets?

## Change The Food

At Performadog and iPurr, we continuously talk about only using ingredients in the food which are sympathetic to the dog. By that, we actually mean the ingredients are required to foster a healthy microbiome, and those ingredients are present in the food at levels that actually **encourage the correct balance of microbiota to restore and maximise the symbiotic relationship between the microbiome and the animal.**

A perfect example of this is the discussion that centres around the use of grains in pet food. More and more products are appearing on the market boasting a **“grain free”** status, with proponents of grain-free diets making a claim that “you never see a dog chewing on a head of wheat”. While this may be true, it doesn’t take into consideration the evolving status of our **domesticated dogs and cats that are now quite capable of digesting starch,** plus the fact that resistant starch is also a valued nutrient for organisms in the large intestine where it is fermented to **produce butyrate**. The other interesting snippet regarding starch is that **all dry foods contain starch, whether they be grain free or grain based.** Grain free foods typically rely on carbohydrate sources such as potato, pea flour and tapioca to provide the starch with which to bind the food together to make a crunchy kibble, whereas foods containing grain use rice or groats or similar for their starch supply. The critical factor here is how much starch is in the food in total, and whether it is balanced to the needs of the microbiome. It goes without saying that excessive amounts of starch, or starch in the wrong balance, **can cause low-level gut inflammation which, as we now know is a precursor to skin and coat issues in our pets.**

## Feed a Pre and Probiotic

The term “probiotic” was first coined by a US researcher to describe the effect of infusing the gut with live, beneficial bacteria. The word soon gained general use as a noun, and is now defined by the **World Health Organisation as “live microorganisms,** which when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host.”Today, there are many pre and probiotic supplements on the market for a variety of applications not only in our dogs and cats but for humans and as a useful additive in the nutrition of many other domesticated animals.

Pre and Probiotics are available in a number of forms; powder, tablets, liquids or gels. Regardless of the form of the pre and probiotic, it should always be remembered that we are dealing with live bacteria. In the case of powders and tablets, the bacteria are in a freeze-dried form, and while being shelf stable, longevity is enhanced through storage in the refrigerator. They are far more stable than the gel or liquid forms which have a relatively short shelf life. Next time you are in the supermarket, check the “use by date” on the yoghurt, and that will give you a good indication of how long these liquid types of probiotics will keep.

## The Benefits of Feeding Pre and Probiotics Are Universally Accepted As Being Helpful In a Number of Situations Including:

* Disease or sensitivity issues such as skin and coat disorders.
* Stress situations – feedlot cattle are often fed **probiotics** on arrival to combat the stress disorder “feedlot fever”.
* After illness to restore gut motility following antibiotic treatment.
* Dietary related issues that require improvement to digestion.
* As a digestive aid in aged dogs and cats where digestive efficiency has declined.
* To assist an animal that is suffering from parasite infection.

Of course, we now know all of these problems are associated with disruptions to the balance of the microbiome, so it shouldn’t come as a big surprise that seeding the gut with beneficial bacteria will make a difference to the health and well-being of our pets.

**Many pet owners have resorted to using yoghurt as an emergency probiotic, but here at performadog and iPurr, we prefer to feed our Purple Carrot, pre and probiotic formulation specifically created for animals. Please see this product on our link called Why Purple.**

### **We call this Purple Boost!**

While the microbiome of dogs, cats and humans are quite similar, a more extensive range of bacteria and yeast appear to be superior to the use of the more limited range found in natural yoghurt and human probiotic supplements. Examples of the type of bacteria to look for when contemplating purchasing a probiotic supplement are:

* Lactobacillus acidophilus
* Lactobacillus plantarum
* Lactobacillus casei
* Lactobacillus salivarius
* Lactobacillus rhamnosus
* Lactobacillus brevis
* Enterococcus faecium
* Bifidobacterium bifidum
* Bifidobacterium lactis

* Streptococcus thermophilus

It would be unusual to find all eleven of these strains in the one preparation, but a good mix of any of the above should be suitable for your dog.

### **You can order your ‘Purple Power’ and Pre/Probiotic Mixture here.**

**Clean up the dog’s environment, both the internal and the external environment.** As touched on earlier, chemicals ingested internally or chemicals in the dog’s surrounding environment can have a detrimental effect on the microbiome. Problematic chemicals and medications include:

## Antibiotics

These medications do not discriminate between good bacteria and harmful bacteria, and while being essential in the treatment of bacterial disease, antibiotics also devastate the population of the microbiome. Feeding a probiotic supplement together with natural food sources that promote a healthy biome is essential following a course of medication.

## Shampoos and Conditioners

Excessive use of shampoos and conditioners, or the use of the wrong types (for example, using human shampoo rather than a canine shampoo) can decimate the skin microbiome, which is closely connected to the gut microbiome via what is called the skin-gut axis. In other words, changes in one microbiome affect the other, and the negative impact on one will translate to the other.

## Parasite Control Medications

Flea, tick and worm medications can have a significant effect on the microbiome, with the resultant modification of the microbiota balance being the precursor to skin and coat problems. Heartworm medication, particularly the injectable form which is administered annually, is a particularly harsh chemical that can cause an over-active immune system to go into meltdown. We never inject for heartworm and aim to use more natural or gentler methods of administering anthelmintic treatments.

## Pollutants

Abound in our environment from air born pollutants to household cleaners and disinfectants. Many of these chemicals are blamed for the decline in microbiome diversity, and their avoidance where possible can only assist in maintaining the health and well-being of our pets.

## Natural Allergens

Many of the dogs we see with skin conditions show a seasonal allergy to grasses and pollen. For dogs suffering this type of problem a quick and easy aid in their treatment is to wipe them down with a damp cloth on returning home from a walk. Just removing the offending irritants from the feet, toes, muzzle and chest can be a great help while we work to get the diet, blood nutrient levels and the microbiome back in balance.

## Stress

We are not the only ones to suffer stress-related disorders. Our pets can also suffer, and the microbiome is probably the first part of the body system to be affected. Stress comes in many forms for our canine companions, with one of the most common being nutritional stress from a poorly balanced diet. Other stresses such as separation anxiety can also impact upon the health and well-being in the same way as previously discussed.

So far, this whole discussion has centred on the relevance and impact of the gut microbiome on the health and well-being of our pets.

## But, This is Only Half of The Story.

While it follows that sympathetic ingredients in the food will give rise to a healthy and well-balanced microbiome, we still have to ensure the nutritional balance within the food accurately matches the dog’s particular needs relative to its age and stage of physiological development.

To achieve this outcome, Performadog and iPurr food ingredients are analysed for their essential nutrient content before the ingredients are mixed and matched to provide the perfect balance of essential nutrients in the correct ratios to one another. This method, known as nutrient ramping **(see the separate article Nutrient Ramping)** ensures the correct levels of nutrients are available for use in the body proportionally to the rate of energy expenditure.

The thrust of this nutritional approach is to identify and optimise each process in delivering essential nutrients to the body by optimising each stage of the entire process.

**What all this means is that the maintenance of good health and well-being is not just a one-dimensional process.** It is the sequence of events whereby the ingredients are matched to the microbiome while the nutrients are matched to the animal. In other words, it is like a team effort with each member of the team optimised for the best possible outcome for both you and your dog, so it’s a bit like turning a team of champions into a champion team!

body: **I want each and every friend of mine, who owns a dog to read this post very carefully and when you are done, I urge you to share it with all your dog related friends. Before you do, please read this post with a question I sent to** Performadog’s Nutritionist Bill Wiadrowski.https://www.facebook.com/PerformadogPremiumDryDogFood/posts/3423147067702603?\_\_tn\_\_=K-R**This is one long post you will want to read to the very end, but here is a bit about us first.**In 2016 Myself (Shannon) and Brad made an informed decision to feed our dogs Performadog and within four weeks we noticed positive changes, at the time we had a 12 year old, 7 year old, 4 year old and an 8 week old puppy. We have been registered ANKC breeders of German Shepherds for over 18 years, Brad has been a RAAF Police Dog Handler for over 21 years, and I myself have a background in the Animal Industry as a Vet Nurse and Dog trainer. It’s always been important to us to provide the very best nutrition to our dogs which led us to Performadog after trying many many brands that are available on the market with no success. So here is a factual story of why we have and will always feed our dogs Performadog from now on.In early 2019 I allowed myself to be influenced by others and social media dog related groups that I shouldn’t be feeding my dogs this or that and I made the decision to change to a different brand of dog food, I will refer to this brand as Food A to prevent any negativity. Boy! That was the worst mistake we could have ever made and cost us a lot more in vet bills and not to mention the stress involved constantly having our dogs with minor health issues.We started to see a decline in our dogs health and condition, we couldn’t keep weight on some of them which required more food and was costing us a fortune as we were advised to add so much more to their bowl and required hours of prep work each month, something Brad and I did not have time for with him working 5 days a week and myself on permanent night shift and 3 school age kids. But we persevered and would prepare a large quantity of raw food just to add to the dry food and although their weight improved that was the only benefit we saw. But we started to question why we needed to add all this extra raw meat, fruit and veggies when the food was supposed to be a complete and healthy diet.This went on for 12 months until we moved interstate and we decided to change yet again to another brand of food (lets refer to this one as Food B) as we no longer had the sources to get our fresh raw products and not knowing if we could get them in the local area.So this new Food B seemed OK, but the amount of food required each day was of concern to us, actually for a couple of our dogs given their lifestyle it seemed extreme and would see us whizz through a 20kg bag in no time. Let’s not talk about how much was coming out the back end either as it seemed more than half of it was being produced as waste.But this Food B, something wasn’t right, I started seeing some significant skin issues in a couple of our dogs, and after making contact with the brand company it was suggested to us that we switch these particular dog to 1 of 2 different products, one was supposedly specifically designed for dogs with skin issues and we couldn’t believe it when after a short period of time it actually made their skin worse and we had to resort to weekly medicated shampoo baths just to relieve them of their conditions. It was a formulated diet that was supposed to alleviate skin irritations…Here is where things get really interesting, in January 2020 one of our females gave birth to a litter of 10 puppies. I was informed that she would be hard to get into whelp due to phytoestrogen in Performadog or so I was told, and it would take at least 18 months after she ceased being fed Performadog that I would be able to consider putting her in whelp. Yet here she was, with a healthy size litter.It was hard to keep weight on her during her pregnancy as the volume of food required just made it too uncomfortable for her in the last two weeks and we were constantly having to feed her to make sure she maintained a healthy weight and for the healthy development of the unborn litter of puppies.Once these puppies were born it became even harder to keep up with her nutritional needs, we fought a very hard battle and I started to question why we were paying so much for a premium brand product that wasn’t doing what it said it would deliver. They had only been on Food B for a short period of time so I decided to give it the benefit of the doubt and keep them on it to see if things improved.I made the huge mistake of weaning puppies to Food B and then eventually onto Food A (we included fresh meat and soft bones they could chew on) thinking surely nothing can go wrong.**THIS IS WHERE IT GETS INTERESTING!!!**From the moment they started on solids they just seem to hover slightly under an ideal weight, and the scratching omg! they always seem to stop in the middle of something and scratch, every time you looked at one they were scratching. It absolutely drove me nuts when i couldn’t find anything significantly wrong with them and nor could our wonderful Vet at their six week health exam.Then at around seven weeks there was one particular puppy who stood out, not just because of her temperament or conformation but for all the wrong reasons. I started to notice slight hair loss, hive-like rash on her abdomen, it had been picked up at the 6 week exam that her lymph glands were slightly enlarged. I had a sneaky feeling of where this was headed and whilst we treated for the itchy skin, a week later out came the angry ear infection.eight weeks old and this poor puppy had so much going wrong with her it was almost unbelievable. The next two weeks were horrific, the angry ear infection had cleared up but now we were dealing with something much more sinister, this poor puppy had swollen lips and ulcer like skin infection that covered her entire mouth (see pictures).We were once again back at the Vets and it was at this time that I knew something had to change. The puppy was prescribed a ten day course of antibiotics and I was to continue with washing and keeping her mouth clean and as dry as possible and no more Chicken. Her skin got worse before it got better and there was a point were I actually expressed a concern for her ongoing health and how severe the reaction was given her age and discussed euthanasia, our awesome Vet advised us to hang in there with her. If this was going to be an ongoing issue this was no life for a dog to live. My other concern was that I needed to remove her from a chicken based food, that in itself was a challenge, given that the majority of dog foods and puppy in particular are made from chicken or chicken by-products.After being at the Vets, I came straight home and began the dreaded search for a food that did not contain chicken. There are so many different foods available on the market, you could spend an entire day looking at the nutritional content and comparing them and the majority of them contained chicken. Then I contacted Kris Kotsopoulos to quiz him on Performadog puppy, satisfied it didn’t have chicken in it. I ordered a 20kg bag and some Purple Boost that day and haven’t looked back since. This puppy hasn’t had any major outbreaks like she did when she was younger, in fact she has the occasional chicken wing or drumstick to chew on without any repercussions, I will let some more recent photos of her speak for themselves.https://www.facebook.com/pg/BrashawinGermanShepherdDogs/photos/?tab=album&album\_id=10156800829541851If you see common recurring issues in your dogs, then the food you are feeding could very well be the cause of the issue. summary: Defines 'holistic' (from J.C. Smuts' holism) and what it means for Performadog and iPurr food.
body:
## Holistic

Is the adjective of the noun “holism”, a term that was first coined by the famous South African academic, military leader and statesman J.C. Smuts, which he described as the **“fundamental factor operative towards the creation of wholes in the universe”.** The word was used by Smuts to designate the tendency in nature to produce organised “wholes” (bodies or organisms) from the ordered grouping of units.

In more recent times the term has been commonly used in medicine to describe the concept of the whole being greater than the sum of the parts, a philosophy that is strongly endorsed by the alternative medicine community, as distinct from the conventional medicine stream that is strongly oriented towards **treating organs in isolation to the balance of the organs in the body.**

It follows, therefore, that holistic food, by definition, must nourish the body as a whole. **Unfortunately, most pet foods carrying the holistic label claim,** merely use the term to describe a food that has been made from natural ingredients. **But making food from natural ingredients in no way guarantees the food ingredients are appropriate for the animal being fed,** nor does it guarantee the nutritional and therapeutic needs of the animal as a whole are being met.

## So, What Does Meet The True Definition of Holistic Food?

Creating food that actually meets the definition of “food as medicine” must meet two basic criteria. Firstly, the ingredients must be appropriate or sympathetic to the animal’s digestive ability, and secondly, the nutrient profile must match the dog’s genetic requirement for nutrients at its particular life stage.

We have made it our priority that Performadog and iPurr Pet foods meet these requirements.
